title: Carbon credit financing emerges as Africa’s biggest bet for expanding clean cooking
summary:
Africa is moving faster to adopt clean cookstovesIn June, the IEA announced Africa had secured $900 million in new financial commitments towards clean cooking technologies.
Advertisement AdvertisementMore than 30 governments in countries accounting for about 80% of Africans who still lack access to clean cooking have introduced 121 new clean cooking policies since the Paris climate summit in 2015, the energy agency said.
Clean cooking is not a luxury, but an everyday necessity affecting every household, Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu said after co-hosting an IEA conference on clean cooking in Dar es Salaam earlier this year.
That followed the African Union's Dar es Salaam Declaration on Clean Cooking, adopted by 30 governments last year.
Advertisement AdvertisementCritics of the approach say relying too heavily on carbon credits to finance clean cooking is still risky.

title: The trick to lowering gas prices is driving less, US energy secretary says
summary:
Americans have been paying some of the highest prices for gas in years since the US attacked Iran in February.
US Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, said, while making the rounds on the Sunday morning news shows, that despite the ongoing conflict, gas prices will soon go down because summer is ending.
"If I had to guess, they're more likely to go down than go up," Wright said of gas prices.
Gas prices first spiked after the US launched a surprise attack on Iran in February, and Iran responded by effectively shutting down the Strait of Hormuz.
The American Automobile Association said Labor Day weekend travelers are seeing the highest gas prices ever for this time of year.

title: Madrid Region and the City of Leganés Launch an Open Call Urban Design Contest for the new “Puerta de Madrid” Sustainable District in Leganés (Madrid)
summary:
Leganés City Council.
Community of Madrid, (Madrid's Regional Government) and the City Council of Leganés have launched an urban planning design contest aimed at obtaining the best planning proposals for the sustainable and innovative development of the new "Puerta de Madrid" district, located adjacent to the north and east of the established Leganés Norte neighbourhood.
This urban development will be managed through a consortium in which both public administrations will participate.
The selected proposals must be fully integrated into the wider urban context and will incorporate advanced criteria in the fields of environmental sustainability, urban innovation, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, climate resilience and social cohesion.
Subsequently, through a procurement procedure, the winning teams will be eligible to compete for the award of a service contract for drafting the planning instrument that will define the urban development framework of the future district.

title: Public consultation launched on plans for new Welsh renewable energy company
summary:
The company would not "replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household electricity prices", it said in a consultation document.
It added that its purpose would be to "help Wales reduce energy costs over time by developing and owning renewable energy assets" and "supporting local and community ownership, investing in smart local energy systems".
It would also "help more organisations use locally generated energy" and try to attract investment into Welsh energy infrastructure.
The consultation looks at establishing a Welsh Energy Wealth Fund to allow energy projects "to support the most vulnerable in Wales as well as those living in areas where projects are being delivered".
The minister said many of the levers for energy are decided at a UK level, but added that energy produced by a public energy company could allow "lower energy prices" through agreements with local large energy users.

title: The Green Energy Paradox: Saving Nature by Destroying It
summary:
AdvertisementAs the Trump administration reverses elements of the previous administration's wind and solar policies, perhaps Americans should ask a question that has been strangely absent from the energy debate: Just how “green” is green energy?
Mining requires enormous quantities of heavy machinery, much of it diesel-powered.
What I object to is the marketing trick whereby one enormous industrial system is described as “dirty,” while another enormous industrial system is painted green and presented as if it descended from heaven on a leaf.
The technology advertised as saving nature requires mines, diesel machinery, steel, concrete, factories, transmission systems, and huge areas of land.
If saving nature requires destroying nature on an industrial scale, perhaps the first thing that needs recycling is our definition of environmentalism.
